subject: radiology
title: X-ray Tube: Cathode, Anode, and Tungsten Target Physics

steps.title: Cathode Filament Construction
steps.tx: **Cathode tungsten filament** coils serve as the primary source of electrons inside the diagnostic X-ray tube. Tungsten is selected specifically because its high atomic number of 74 and extraordinary melting point of 3422 degrees Celsius withstand high thermal stress without vaporizing. Operating in an electrical filament circuit, the tungsten wire is heated to white incandescence by currents between 3 and 6 amperes, liberating abundant free electrons.

rows: High electron density and emission efficiency
Prevents filament burn-out at high heat loads
Maintains tube vacuum without gas fouling
Enables winding into durable thin coils

steps.tx: Two filaments in one tube give the radiographer a choice between sharpness and load. A **dual focus tube** carries small and large tungsten filaments in a molybdenum focusing cup: the small filament for fine detail at low current, the large one spreading heat for heavy exposures. Selecting focus is therefore selecting what the image is allowed to be. The cup shape keeps the electron stream aimed at the same track on the anode.
steps.say: Dual focus tubes hold small and large filaments in a focusing cup. Small gives detail; large spreads heat for heavy exposures.

vis.alt: Diagram of a dual focus X-ray tube cathode with two tungsten filaments in a molybdenum cup.
vis.caption: Two tungsten filaments of different sizes sit inside a molybdenum focusing cup. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Focusing Cup Dynamics
steps.tx: **Molybdenum focusing cup** structures house the filament coils within a recessed metal cavity. Because boiling electrons naturally repel one another, an unconfined electron cloud would disperse widely across the tube chamber. The cup is maintained at a negative electrical potential relative to the cathode filament, electrostatically repelling and condensing the divergent electron stream into a narrow, parallel beam directed precisely toward the anode focal track.

left.title: Unfocused Electron Cloud
points: Strikes non-target areas of anode disc
Degrades image sharpness with severe penumbra

right.title: Focusing Cup Beam
points: Focuses beam tightly onto target focal spot
Maintains fine radiographic detail and contrast

steps.title: Dual Focal Spot Engineering
steps.tx: **Dual focus spot selection** provides clinicians with two distinct operational filaments mounted side by side. The small filament projects an effective focal spot measuring 0.6 millimetres for high-resolution imaging of thin peripheral extremities, restricted to low tube currents under 300 milliamperes. Conversely, the large filament projects a 1.2-millimetre focal spot capable of accepting heavy heat loads up to 1000 milliamperes for dense abdominal exposures.

rows: Fine bony detail in extremities and skull
Thick body parts like abdomen, pelvis, and lumbar spine

steps.title: Rotating Anode Architecture
steps.tx: **Rotating anode design** overcomes the severe thermal limitations of historic stationary targets. In diagnostic tubes, over 99 percent of electron kinetic energy transforms into waste heat, with less than 1 percent yielding useful X-radiation. Modern tubes employ a bevelled disc rotated by an induction motor at speeds between 3000 and 10000 revolutions per minute, spreading intense heat over a wide circular focal track.

left.title: Stationary Anode System
points: Fixed tungsten button embedded in copper
Heat concentrates on a single static spot
Restricted to dental and portable units

right.title: Rotating Anode System
points: Molybdenum disc rotating at 3000 to 10000 RPM
Heat distributes over a circular focal ring
Tolerates high tube currents for CT and radiography

steps.title: Tungsten-Rhenium Target Metallurgy
steps.tx: **Tungsten-rhenium focal track** alloys compose the target face bombarded by incoming electrons. Pure tungsten tends to craze and form microscopic fissures under repetitive thermal cycling from room temperature to over 1000 degrees Celsius. Adding 5 to 10 percent rhenium improves mechanical elasticity and thermal shock resistance, preventing focal track pitting and preserving consistent X-ray output over thousands of patient exposures.

rows: Lightweight structural support and heat storage

steps.title: The Line Focus Principle
steps.tx: **Line focus principle** geometry resolves the conflicting demands of high thermal capacity and sharp spatial resolution. By angling the anode target between 7 and 20 degrees, the area bombarded by electrons, known as the actual focal spot, remains large to absorb heat. However, the projected effective focal spot viewed from the patient remains small, calculated as the actual spot multiplied by the sine of target angle.

nodes.label: Large actual focal spot absorbs heat
Bevelled anode angle projects small spot

steps.tx: An angled target lets a tube cheat geometry on behalf of the image. The **line focus principle** makes the electron footprint large where heat lands, the actual focal spot, while the projected effective spot seen by the patient stays small and sharp. Anode angle is the compromise dial between heat capacity and resolution. Every specification sheet quoting focal spot size is quoting the effective spot, a detail worth knowing before criticising an image.
steps.say: The line focus principle projects a small effective spot from a large heated footprint. Anode angle balances sharpness against heat capacity.

vis.alt: Geometry diagram of the line focus principle showing actual versus effective focal spot.
vis.caption: An angled anode shows a long heated track projecting a small effective focal spot. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Anode Stem and Thermal Dissipation
steps.tx: **Anode stem thermal isolation** protects delicate rotor bearings from destructive conduction heat. The anode disc mounts to a slender molybdenum neck whose narrow cross-section and modest thermal conductivity restrict heat flow into the copper rotor sleeve. Heat dissipation from the disc proceeds predominantly by infrared thermal radiation across the vacuum into the surrounding dielectric insulating oil, which circulates within the grounded lead tube housing.

left.title: Anode Disc Dissipation
points: Absorbed by surrounding dielectric oil bath

right.title: Molybdenum Neck Barrier
points: Slender stem restricts conductive heat transfer
Protects steel rotor ball bearings from seizing
Maintains smooth rotation at high RPM speeds

steps.title: Tube Housing and Leakage Shielding
steps.tx: **Evacuated tube envelope** housing maintains a vacuum of ten to the minus six torr, preventing projectile electrons from colliding with gas atoms and losing velocity before reaching the anode. Heavy lead sheeting encloses the housing to absorb isotropically scattered leakage radiation. Regulatory standards mandate that leakage radiation escaping through the housing must not exceed 1 milligray per hour measured at a distance of 1 metre.
